doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Fearlessness, faith and musicians who quit
summary: Jeannie says musicians need fearlessness and faith, describes a seven-year period in which musicians resign themselves to quitting, and calls for a support system.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Do you find that some of your students have more success simply because of their personalities? That they’re more easy going or willing to take chances?
Yeah, yeah. Well because that’s that freedom we speak about in terms of personal expression again you see.
And that comes from having confidence.

And I think — I don’t think you could teach anybody that. I think a lot of their early life experiences with their folks and maybe even before they’re born, I think there’s a heck of a lot to even deal with that. Because most real fearful people, they can accomplish a lot in another direction, but I don’t think they can be a musician. Not a jazz musician, and be that fearful. It has something also to do with faith.

Like someplace, somewhere, somebody needs a good band? Because you just have to feel like tomorrow’s going to be okay. And then there comes the other side, like you go up that mountain, and you go along, and you’re on the road and you’re thinking next gig, whatever. Then you get to a point in everybody’s life where you start feeling, I don’t know if I can do that. And a lot of it has to do with the physical body. If they’ve taken care of it or all of a sudden they get a little twinge here or there, and they start losing that faith. And that’s when you see them putting the horns behind the bed or in the closet, and try to find something else to do. Now I’ll tell you, in my experience I’ve found that — to

be a crucible for every musician. I don’t care whether he’s classical or Gospel or a jazz musician. There comes a time when you have to decide whether you’re going to really continue. And to a musician, they have to play — like to play. See jazz musicians have to play, they always say that. Every musician comes to that point in his life where he has to decide whether he’s going to continue. And Jimmy and I have been around here long enough to know when they’re really struggling with that. Because it doesn’t happen overnight. It happens over a period, I’ve found, of about seven years. On again, off again, on again. Toward the end of that seven years, it seems to be more off than on, but they seem to resign themselves. It takes about seven years for them to resign themself to the fact that they’re no longer going to either keep up with what’s going on, or want to stay on the road, or want to put up with the diminishing physical. And that is so — it’s a sad thing. We’ve seen it all up and down the road playing different places.
And really in a sense it’s something — well it’s not equal to — but in a sense it’s like dealing with a thoroughbred horse.
He’s geared to run in that race you know.
And that’s what it lives for you see.

And then pretty soon it can’t. And I don’t know, I guess it’s just like boxers or anything else. There comes a time, but I think we need more — what can I say — I say we need more places for people like us to talk, to go and talk this thing, before it happens. So that at least the preparation won’t be so terrible. I don’t know what you would call it, but I think we need a place, where musicians can go and talk about that.
We need some support in dealing.

Some kind of support system, in the musical — among musicians — so that they can say well I can call, not a Reverend Gensel, because he just passed, but I mean a group of people that have been there, that have decided how they managed that, how they came away from it with grace, and how to maintain your personage. And that’s the one thing I find the saddest thing, that I’ve seen, as long as I’ve been playing. Forty years I’ve been playing. And that’s the saddest thing. When you see them quit. “Oh I’m not playing anymore” and that. But they need support. And I think we should really have a place, or some organization or something where a guy can go, or a woman, when they decide to stop their life’s work.
